After the evening prayer at the village temple, Shalini pulled Sarika behind the flower stall.
"My cousin from Nashik wants your number. He saw you at the fair. Just give it, na? And don't tell your Amma, she'll make a big thing."
Sarika's fingers tightened on her dupatta. "I'm not comfortable giving my number to someone I don't know."
"Don't be so boring. He's nice. I promised him."
"Then that's your promise. Not mine. No."
Shalini rolled her eyes and walked off in a huff.
Walking home along the canal, Sarika kept thinking about "don't tell your Amma." That was the part that felt wrong.
At dinner she told Amma everything. Amma listened, put a hand on her head and said, "You did right. Both times." That same night she went next door and spoke to Shalini's mother, calmly, about the cousin.

One day behind the science block he told me that two seniors had been taking his money every week and saying they'd hurt him if he told. Then he said, "Swear you won't say anything. Swear on our friendship."

He thanked me, called Karthik out of class right then, and went with him to the principal before school ended. He phoned Karthik's parents that evening.

Ira, you think your generation invented confusing signals? Sit, let your Jyoti Masi tell you about missed calls.
